Lichess Chess Game Analytics

Patterns of Victory, Openings, and Player Dynamics — A comprehensive analysis of over 20,000 Lichess chess games exploring win rates, opening strategies, rating dynamics, and game outcome patterns.

Dataset: 20,058 games Source: Lichess.org via Kaggle Analysis Date: May 2026

The dataset contains 20,058 chess games from Lichess.org. Of these, 80.5% were rated games (16,155), where outcomes affected players' Elo ratings. The remaining 19.5% (3,903) were casual games.

Figure 1.1: Distribution of game outcomes. White won 10,001 games (49.9%), Black won 9,107 (45.4%), and 950 games (4.7%) ended in draws.
Figure 1.2: How games ended. Resignation is the most common conclusion at 55.6%, followed by checkmate at 31.5%.

Among decisive games (excluding draws), White won 52.3% — a clear but not overwhelming advantage. The resignation rate of 55.6% dominates, meaning most games end by a player conceding, not by checkmate (31.5%) or timeout (8.4%). The draw rate of 4.5% is consistent with online play at mixed skill levels.

Figure 1.3: Distribution of game length in half-moves. The mean is 60 turns; the distribution is heavily right-skewed with a long tail of marathon games.

2. White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

+4.7 pp
White Advantage (percentage points)

White-to-Black Win Ratio
19,108
Decisive Games Analyzed

Among 19,108 decisive games (excluding draws), White wins 52.3% to Black's 47.7%. This +4.7 percentage-point edge is statistically robust and aligns with the long-established chess literature on first-move advantage (typically cited at +2–6 pp). On Lichess across mixed skill levels, White wins roughly 1.10 games for every Black win.

2.1 White Advantage by Victory Condition

Figure 2.1: White's win rate broken down by how the game ended. The advantage is most pronounced in checkmates, where White wins 52.9% of the time.

White's edge is strongest in checkmates (52.9%), suggesting the first-move advantage translates most directly into superior attacking positions. In resignations, White wins 52.4% — an edge but narrower. In timeout games, White wins 49.7%, likely because White often holds a time advantage or better position when the clock runs down.

2.2 White Advantage by Rating Tier

Figure 2.2: White's win rate across six rating brackets. The dashed line shows the overall average of 52.3%.

White's advantage varies notably by skill level. At lower ratings (<1200), the edge is 52.7%. This narrows at intermediate levels but widens again at higher ratings. At the 2000+ level, White wins 50.6%, suggesting stronger players convert the opening initiative more effectively.

2.3 White Advantage by Time Control

Figure 2.3: White's advantage across time control categories, from fastest to slowest.

In faster time controls — UltraBullet and Bullet — White's advantage is at its smallest (45.1% and 52.0% respectively), suggesting that at extreme speeds, speed and intuition dominate over the structural advantage of the first move. In Classical games, White's edge peaks at 53.8%, confirming that deeper thinking allows White to convert the initiative more effectively.

2.4 The Combined Effect: Heatmap

Figure 2.4: White win rate as a function of both time control and rating bracket. Darker blue = stronger White advantage; red tones = where Black performs better.

The interaction between rating and time control is revealing. In Classical games at the 2000+ level, White's advantage can reach extremely high levels, while in faster controls across lower ratings, the win rates are closer to parity. This two-dimensional view confirms that both skill and thinking time amplify White's positional edge.

Figure 3.1: Distribution of Elo ratings for White and Black players. Both distributions are centered similarly, with White players having a slightly higher mean (1597 vs. 1589).

The rating distributions for White and Black players are broadly similar, with means of 1597 and 1589 respectively and standard deviations of ~291 Elo. The range spans from approximately 784 to 2700, typical of online chess platforms.

3.1 Rating Differential: The Dominant Predictor

Figure 3.2: White's win probability as a function of the rating differential (White − Black). Negative differentials mean Black is higher-rated.

The rating differential is the single strongest predictor of game outcome. When White out-rates Black by more than 400 points, White's win probability surges to 88.3%. Conversely, when Black out-rates White by over 400 points, White wins only 15.9% of games. The relationship is nearly linear in the center (±200 Elo), with each 100-point rating advantage translating to approximately a 10–15 percentage-point shift in win probability.

3.2 Victory Type by Rating Bracket

Figure 3.3: Checkmate rate, resignation rate, and draw rate by rating bracket.

Higher-rated players are far more likely to win by resignation than by checkmate. At the 2000+ level, the resign rate reaches 67.8% while the checkmate rate drops to 14.4%. Lower-rated players (<1200) see more checkmates (39.8%) — reflecting the tendency of beginners to play positions out to mate rather than resigning. Draw rates increase sharply with rating: from 5.1% at the lowest tier to 8.0% at the highest, consistent with higher-level play producing more balanced, accurately defended positions.

Figure 3.4: Average game length (half-moves) by how the game ended. Drawn games are the longest; timeout games the shortest.

4.2 Openings Where Black Outperforms White

Figure 4.4: Openings where Black's win rate exceeds White's (minimum 20 games played). These are relatively rare and typically involve sharp, counter-attacking lines.

These openings are characterized by aggressive Black setups that challenge White's center control early. They represent a smaller fraction of total games — the overwhelming majority of openings still favor White — but they demonstrate that specific opening choices can negate or even reverse the first-move advantage.

4.3 Opening Depth and Outcomes

Figure 4.5: How opening length (in half-moves) relates to White win rate and draw rate. The red line shows game counts at each depth.

Deeper opening theory (more book moves played) correlates with a slightly higher draw rate and more balanced outcomes — a reflection of players who both know theory reaching more equal positions. Shallow openings (1–2 moves of book) often arise from off-beat lines or early blunders, leading to more decisive results. The majority cluster around 3–9 half-moves of opening play.

The data reveals a clear pattern: as time controls lengthen, games become longer, checkmates become rarer, and draws become more common. Classical games average 55 turns with a draw rate of 7.0%, while Bullet games average only 58 turns with a draw rate of 4.1%.

Time pressure dominates fast formats: UltraBullet sees 12.8% of games end by timeout, compared to just 3.7% in Classical. This underscores that in faster formats, clock management is as important as chess skill. The resignation rate is highest in Blitz (54.3%), where positions become objectively lost before flags fall.

6. Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

This synthesis distills the most actionable insights from the analysis of 20,058 Lichess chess games. A coach, platform analyst, or serious player should take away the following:

  1. White's First-Move Advantage Is Real but Modest: White wins 52.3% of decisive games — a +4.7pp edge. This is consistent across all segments and validates the classical chess understanding. However, the edge is not insurmountable: Black still wins 47.7% of the time, and specific counter-attacking openings can negate or even reverse the advantage.
  2. Rating Differential Dwarfs Color Advantage: The most powerful predictor of outcome is the Elo gap between players, not who moves first. A 200+ point rating advantage translates to a roughly 80%+ win probability for the higher-rated player, regardless of color. White's first-move advantage contributes roughly the equivalent of a 35–50 Elo point edge.
  3. Time Control Fundamentally Shapes Chess: In Bullet and UltraBullet, clock handling and flagging dominate — 12.8% of UltraBullet games end by timeout. In Classical, only 3.7% do, while draws rise to 7.0%. Faster chess is not just "speed chess" — it rewards a different skill set centered on intuition and time management.
  4. Higher-Rated Players Play Longer, Draw More, Mate Less: As rating increases, games last more moves, end in checkmate less often, and produce more draws. At 2000+, 8.0% of games are drawn and only 14.4% end in checkmate — players resign in lost positions well before mate is delivered. At lower ratings, mates are common (39.8%).
  5. Opening Choice Matters, but Marginally: The most popular openings (Sicilian Defense, Queen's Pawn Game, Italian Game) show White win rates close to the 52.3% overall average. The openings that deviate most are either sharp gambits (higher White win rates) or hypermodern/counter-attacking setups (higher Black win rates). For most club-level players, time spent on tactics and endgames will yield more Elo points than memorizing rare opening lines.
  6. White Advantage Amplifies with Time and Skill: In Classical games at the 2000+ level, White's win rate is highest. The first-move advantage is most effectively converted when players have both the time and skill to capitalize on the initiative. At lower ratings and faster controls, randomness and mistakes dilute the edge.
  7. The Modern Online Chess Game Is Decided by Resignation: 55.6% of all games end in resignation, not checkmate. This is consistent across all but the fastest time controls and reflects the online etiquette of conceding lost positions rather than forcing the opponent to deliver mate — a cultural norm that differs from over-the-board play at amateur levels.

6.1 Recommendations for Players

  • As White: Play principled openings that maintain the initiative. The data shows White's edge is convertible, especially in longer time controls. Don't squander it on speculative attacks in fast games.
  • As Black: Learn at least one reliable defense against e4 and d4. The Sicilian and French Defense appear frequently and offer counter-attacking chances. The data confirms specific openings where Black actually outperforms White — these are worth studying.
  • For Improvement: Focus on the middle game and time management. The overwhelming predictor of victory is rating differential (i.e., skill gap), not opening choice. Reducing blunders and using the clock wisely matters more than opening memorization.

6.2 Recommendations for Platform Analysts

  • Monitor the draw rate by time control category over time — rising draw rates at faster controls could indicate engine-assisted play.
  • Track the White win rate as a benchmark for rating system calibration; significant deviations from ~52% could indicate rating inflation or pairing algorithm issues.
  • The heavy concentration of resignations (vs. checkmates) suggests that anti-cheat systems should focus on move quality in the mid-game rather than only detecting unnatural terminal positions.
